Main.sentence: The Chicago White Sox are an American professional ___E:baseball U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball)___ team based in ___E:Chicago U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago)___ .

The White Sox won their first World Series, the ___E:1906 World Series U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1906_World_Series)___ against the Cubs, with a defense-oriented team dubbed "the Hitless Wonders", and later won the ___E:1917 World Series U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1917_World_Series)___ against the ___E:New York Giants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Giants)___ .

From 1951 to 1967, the White Sox had their longest period of sustained success, scoring a winning record for 17 straight seasons.

Over the years, the White Sox have become noted for many of their ___E:uniform U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball_uniform)___ innovations and changes.
In 1960, they became the first team in the major sports to put players' last names on ___E:jerseys U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey_(clothing)#In_sports)___ for identification purposes.

In 1912, the White Sox debuted a large "S" in a Roman-style ___E:font U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Font)___ , with a small "O" inside the top loop of the "S" and a small "X" inside the bottom loop. With a couple of brief interruptions, the dark-blue logo with the large "S" lasted through 1938 (but continued in a modified block style into the 1940s).
Through the 1940s, the White Sox team colors were primarily navy blue trimmed with red.

The White Sox logo in the 1950s and 1960s (actually beginning in the 1949 season) was the word "SOX" in ___E:Gothic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackletter)___ script, diagonally arranged, with the "S" larger than the other two letters.
From 1949 through 1963, the primary color was black (trimmed with red after 1951).
This is the logo associated with the Go-Go Sox era.

In 1964, the primary color went back to navy blue, and the road uniforms changed from gray to pale blue. In 1971, the team's primary color changed from royal blue to red, with the color of their ___E:pinstripes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinstripes)___ and ___E:caps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball_cap)___ changing to red. The 1971–1975 uniform included red ___E:socks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball_uniform#Stockings_and_pants)___ .
In 1976, the team's uniforms changed again.

The team's primary color changed back from red to navy. The team based their uniforms on a style worn in the early days of the franchise, with white jerseys worn at home, and blue on the ___E:road U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_(sports))___ .
The team brought back white socks for the last time in team history.
The socks featured a different stripe pattern every year. The team also had the option to wear blue or white pants with either jersey.
Additionally, the team's "SOX" logo was changed to a modern-looking "SOX" in a bold font, with "CHICAGO" written across the jersey.
Finally, the team's logo featured a ___E:silhouette U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silhouette)___ of a batter over the words "SOX".
The new uniforms also featured ___E:collars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collar_(clothing))___ and were designed to be worn untucked — both unprecedented.

Yet by far, the most unusual wrinkle was the option to wear shorts, which the White Sox did for the first game of a ___E:doubleheader U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubleheader_(baseball))___ against the ___E:Kansas City Royals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Royals)___ in 1976. The ___E:Hollywood Stars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Stars)___ of the ___E:Pacific Coast League U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Coast_League)___ had previously tried the same concept, but it was also poorly received.
Apart from aesthetic issues, as a practical matter, shorts are not conducive to sliding, due to the likelihood of significant abrasions.

Upon taking over the team in 1980, new owners Eddie Einhorn and Jerry Reinsdorf announced a contest where fans were invited to create new uniforms for the White Sox. The winning entries, submitted by a fan, had the word "SOX" written across the front of the jersey in the same font as the cap, inside of a large blue stripe trimmed with red. The red and blue stripes were also on the sleeves, and the road jerseys were gray to the home whites.
In those jerseys, the White Sox won 99 games and the AL West championship in 1983, the best record in the majors.
After five years, those uniforms were retired and replaced with a more basic uniform that had "White Sox" written across the front in script, with "Chicago" on the front of the road jersey.
The cap logo was also changed to a cursive "C", although the batter logo was retained for several years.

For a midseason 1990 game at Comiskey Park, the White Sox appeared once in a uniform based on that of the 1917 White Sox. They then switched their regular uniform style once more. In September, for the final series at the old Comiskey Park, the White Sox rolled out a new logo, a simplified version of the 1949–63 Gothic "SOX" logo. They also introduced a uniform with black pinstripes, also similar to the Go-Go Sox era uniform.

The team's primary color changed back to black, this time with silver trim. The team also introduced a new sock logo—a white silhouette of a sock centered inside a white outline of a baseball diamond—which appeared as a sleeve patch on the away uniform until 2010 (switched to the "SOX" logo in 2011), and on the alternate black uniform since 1993. With minor modifications (i.e., occasionally wearing vests, black game jerseys), the White Sox have used this style ever since.

In the 2014 season, the "Winning Ugly" throwbacks were promoted to full-time alternate status, and are now worn at home on Sundays.

In one game during the 2014 season, the Sox paired their throwbacks with a cap featuring the batter logo instead of the wordmark "SOX"; this is currently their batting-practice cap prior to games in the throwback uniforms.
After the 2023 season, the Sunday throwback uniforms were quietly taken off the team's uniform rotation.

In 1979, he was the recipient of the ___E:Ford Frick Award U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Frick_Award)___ , and his profile is permanently on display in the ___E:National Baseball Hall of Fame U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Baseball_Hall_of_Fame)___ .
After the 1966 season, radio rights shifted from WCFL to ___E:WMAQ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WMAQ_(AM))___ (670).

An ___E:NBC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC)___ -owned and -operated station until 1988 when ___E:Westinghouse Broadcasting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westinghouse_Broadcasting)___ purchased it after NBC's withdrawal from radio, it was the home of the Sox until the 1996 season, outside of a team nadir in the early '70s, where it was forced to ___E:broker time U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brokered_programming)___ on suburban ___E:La Grange U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Grange,_Illinois)___ 's ___E:WTAQ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WRDZ_(AM))___ (1300) and ___E:Evanston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evanston,_Illinois)___ 's ___E:WEAW-FM U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WOJO)___ (105.1) to have their play-by-play air in some form (though WEAW transmitted from the ___E:John Hancock Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hancock_Center)___ , FM radio was not established as a band for sports play-by-play at the time),  and a one-season contract on ___E:WBBM U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WBBM_(AM))___ (780) in 1981. After Elson's retirement in 1970, ___E:Harry Caray U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Caray)___ began his tenure as the voice of the White Sox, on radio and on television.
Although best remembered as a broadcaster for the rival Cubs, Caray was very popular with White Sox fans, pining for a "cold one" during broadcasts.
Caray often broadcast from the stands, sitting at a table set up amid the bleachers.
It became a badge of honor among Sox fans to "Buy Harry a beer..." By game's end, one would see a large stack of empty beer cups beside his microphone.

This only endeared him to fans that much more. In fact, he started his tradition of leading the fans in the singing of " ___E:Take Me Out To The Ballgame U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_Me_Out_To_The_Ballgame)___ " with the Sox.  Caray, alongside color analyst ___E:Jimmy Piersall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Piersall)___ , was never afraid to criticize the Sox, which angered numerous Sox managers and players, notably ___E:Bill Melton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Melton)___ and ___E:Chuck Tanner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Tanner)___ .
He left to succeed ___E:Jack Brickhouse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Brickhouse)___ as the voice of the Cubs in 1981, where he became a national icon.

The White Sox shifted through several announcers in the 1980s, before hiring ___E:John Rooney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rooney_(sportscaster))___ as play-by-play announcer in 1989. In 1992, he was paired with color announcer ___E:Ed Farmer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Farmer)___ .
In 14 seasons together, the duo became a highly celebrated announcing team, even being ranked by USA Today as the top broadcasting team in the American League.
Starting with Rooney and Farmer's fifth season together, Sox games returned to the 1000 AM frequency for the first time in 30 years.
By then, it had become the ___E:ESPN owned and operated U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN_Radio)___ ___E:WMVP U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WMVP_(AM))___ .
The last game on WMVP was game 4 of the 2005 World Series, with the White Sox clinching their first World Series title in 88 years.
That also was Rooney's last game with the Sox, as he left to join the radio broadcast team of the St. Louis Cardinals.

In 2006, radio broadcasts returned to 670 AM, this time on the ___E:sports radio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_radio)___ station ___E:WSCR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSCR)___ owned by ___E:CBS Radio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Radio)___ (WSCR took over the 670 frequency in August 2000 as part of a number of shifts among CBS Radio properties to meet market ownership caps).

Ed Farmer became the play-by-play man after Rooney left, joined in the booth by ___E:Chris Singleton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Singleton_(baseball))___ from 2006 to 2007 and then ___E:Steve Stone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Stone_(baseball))___ in 2008. In 2009, ___E:Darrin Jackson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darrin_Jackson)___ became the color announcer for White Sox radio, where he remains today.
Farmer and Jackson were joined by pregame/postgame host Chris Rogney.
The ___E:Chicago White Sox Radio Network U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_White_Sox_Radio_Network)___ currently has 18 affiliates in three states.

As of recently, White Sox games are also broadcast in Spanish with play-by-play announcer ___E:Hector Molina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hector_Molina&action=edit&redlink=1)___ joined in the booth by Billy Russo.

Formerly broadcasting on ___E:ESPN Deportes Radio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN_Deportes_Radio)___ via ___E:WNUA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WCHI-FM)___ , games are now broadcast in Spanish on ___E:WRTO U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WRTO_(AM))___ (1200).

In the 2016 season, the play-by-play rights shifted to ___E:Cumulus Media U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumulus_Media)___ 's ___E:WLS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WLS_(AM))___ (890) under a five-year deal, when WSCR acquired the rights to Cubs games after a one-year period on WBBM. However, by all counts, the deal was a disaster for the White Sox, as WLS's declining ___E:conservative talk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_talk)___ format, associated ratings, and management/personnel issues (including said hosts barely promoting the team and its games), and a signal that is weak in the northern suburbs and into ___E:Wisconsin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin)___ , was not a good fit for the team. Cumulus also had voluminous financial issues, and by the start of 2018, looked to both file ___E:Chapter 11 bankruptcy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_11_bankruptcy)___ and restructure their play-by-play deals or depart them, both with local teams and nationally through their ___E:Westwood One/NFL U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_on_Westwood_One_Sports)___ deal.

The White Sox and ___E:Tribune Broadcasting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribune_Broadcasting)___ (which has since merged with ___E:Nexstar Media Group U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nexstar_Media_Group)___ ) then announced a three-year deal for WGN Radio to become the White Sox flagship as of February 14, 2018, just in time for ___E:spring training U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_training)___ .
Ed Farmer and Darrin Jackson continued to be on play-by-play, with ___E:Andy Masur U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Masur)___ taking over pregame/postgame duties.

Ed Farmer died suddenly on April 1, 2020, a long-term battle with ___E:polycystic kidney disease U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polycystic_kidney_disease)___ , but the team waited to announce his successor due to the ___E:COVID-19 pandemic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic)___ and the uncertainty of the ___E:2020 season U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Major_League_Baseball_season)___ going forward.
On June 30 with the season's structure announced, Masur was confirmed as Farmer's successor for the season.
Under Nexstar's new management, WGN decided to pursue a thriftier programming direction, and made no moves to renew the deal at the end of the 2020 season.

The team thus returned to ___E:WMVP U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WMVP)___ (now managed by ___E:Good Karma Brands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Karma_Brands)___ , which also owns ___E:Brewers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee_Brewers)___ flagship ___E:WTMJ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WTMJ_(AM))___ ) for a multi-year agreement to start with the 2021 season.

In a surprising turn of events, WMVP and the team announced on December 4, 2020, that ___E:Len Kasper U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Len_Kasper)___ , the longtime television play-by-play voice of the Cubs, would move to the South Side and become the radio play-by-play voice of the White Sox. The agreement has flexibility which allows Kasper to do some television games on NBC Sports Chicago on days when Jason Benetti has other national commitments.

White Sox games appeared sporadically on television throughout the first half of the 20th century, most commonly announced by Jack Brickhouse on ___E:WGN-TV U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGN-TV)___ (channel 9).

Starting in 1968, ___E:Jack Drees U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Drees)___ took play-by-play duties as the Sox were broadcast on ___E:WFLD U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WFLD)___ (channel 32).

After 1972, Harry Caray (joined by Jimmy Piersall in 1977) began double duty as a TV and radio announcer for the Sox, as broadcasts were moved to channel 44, ___E:WSNS-TV U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSNS-TV)___ , from 1972 to 1980, followed by one year on WGN-TV.

___E:Don Drysdale U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Drysdale)___ became the play-by-play announcer in 1982, as the White Sox began splitting their broadcasts between WFLD and the new regional ___E:cable television U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_television)___ network, ___E:Sportsvision U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FSN_Chicago)___ .

Ahead of its time, Sportsvision had a chance to gain huge profits for the Sox. However, few people would subscribe to the channel after being used to free-to-air broadcasts for many years, along with Sportsvision being stunted by the city of Chicago's wiring for cable television taking much longer than many markets because of it being an area where over-the-air subscription services were still more popular, resulting in the franchise losing around $300,000 a month.

While this was going on, every Cubs game was on WGN, with Harry Caray becoming the national icon he never was with the White Sox. The relatively easy near-national access to Cubs games versus Sox games in this era, combined with the popularity of Caray and the Cubs being owned by the ___E:Tribune Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribune_Company)___ , is said by some to be the main cause of the Cubs' advantage in popularity over the Sox.

Three major changes to White Sox broadcasting occurred in 1989-1991: in 1989, with the city finally fully wired for cable service, Sportsvision was replaced by SportsChannel Chicago (itself eventually turning into ___E:Fox Sports Net U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Sports_Networks)___ Chicago), which varied over its early years as a premium sports service and basic cable channel.

In 1990, over-the-air broadcasts shifted back to WGN. And in 1991, ___E:Ken Harrelson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Harrelson)___ became the play-by-play announcer of the White Sox.  One of the most polarizing figures in baseball, "Hawk" has been both adored and scorned for his emotive announcing style.
His history of calling out umpires has earned him reprimands from the MLB commissioner's office, and he has been said to be the most biased announcer in baseball.
However, Harrelson has said that he is proud of being "the biggest homer in baseball", saying that he is a White Sox fan like his viewers.

The team moved from FSN Chicago to the newly launched ___E:NBC Sports Chicago U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Sports_Chicago)___ in March 2005, as Jerry Reinsdorf looked to control the rights for his team rather than sell rights to another party; Reinsdorf holds a 40% interest in the network, with 20% of that interest directly owned by the White Sox corporation.

Previously, White Sox local television broadcasts were split between two channels: the majority of games were broadcast on cable by NBC Sports Chicago, and remaining games were produced by ___E:WGN Sports U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGN_Sports)___ and were broadcast locally on WGN-TV. WGN games were also occasionally picked up by local stations in Illinois, Iowa, and Indiana.

In the past, WGN games were broadcast nationally on the ___E:WGN America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGN_America)___ superstation, but those broadcasts ended after the 2014 season as WGN America began its transition to a standard cable network.

WGN Sports-produced White Sox games not carried by WGN-TV were carried by ___E:WCIU-TV U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WCIU-TV)___ (channel 26) until the 2015 season, when they moved to ___E:MyNetworkTV U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MyNetworkTV)___ station ___E:WPWR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WPWR)___ (channel 50).
That arrangement ended on September 1, 2016, when WGN became an independent station.

Prior to 2016, the announcers were the same no matter where the games were broadcast: Harrelson provided play-by-play, and ___E:Steve Stone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Stone_(baseball))___ provided color analysis since 2009.  Games that are broadcast on NBC Sports Chicago feature pregame and postgame shows, hosted by Chuck Garfein with analysis from Bill Melton and occasionally Frank Thomas.

In 2016, the team announced an official split of the play-by-play duties, with Harrelson calling road games and the ___E:Crosstown Series U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosstown_Series)___ and ___E:Jason Benetti U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Benetti)___ calling home games.
In 2017, the team announced that the 2018 season will be Harrelson's final in the booth.
He will call 20 games over the course of the season, after which Benetti will take over full-time play-by-play duties.

On January 2, 2019, the White Sox (along with the ___E:Chicago Bulls U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bulls)___ and ___E:Chicago Blackhawks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Blackhawks)___ ) agreed to an exclusive multiyear deal with NBC Sports Chicago, ending the team's broadcasts on WGN-TV following the ___E:2019 season U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Chicago_White_Sox_season)___ .

Prior to the 2024 season, the White Sox named ___E:John Schriffen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Schriffen)___ as its new lead television play-by-play announcer, after Benetti departed to join the ___E:Detroit Tigers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Tigers)___ broadcast team.
For the 2025 season, the White Sox moved to ___E:Chicago Sports Network U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Sports_Network)___ , a new regional sports network.
